title: “And, Carpenter, what is the practice that leads to the abandoning of unwholesome thoughts? Here, a monk awakens desire, makes effort, arouses energy, applies his…
content: “And, Carpenter, what is the practice that leads to the abandoning of unwholesome thoughts? Here, a monk awakens desire, makes effort, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives so that unarisen evil, unwholesome states do not arise … so that arisen evil, unwholesome states are abandoned … so that unarisen wholesome states arise … so that arisen wholesome states are maintained, not confused, increased, expanded, developed, and fulfilled. Such is the practice that leads to the abandoning of unwholesome thoughts.”

title: “And how, monks, is a monk ‘knowing and understanding’? He has known and understood evil, unwholesome states that are defiling, leading to renewed existence, fearful,…
content: “And how, monks, is a monk ‘knowing and understanding’? He has known and understood evil, unwholesome states that are defiling, leading to renewed existence, fearful, producing painful results, leading to future birth, aging, and death. Thus, monks, a monk is ‘knowing and understanding.’”

title: Standing to one side, the deity Uttara recited this verse in the presence of the Blessed One: Life is swept along, Short is the lifespan…
content:
Standing to one side, the deity Uttara recited this verse in the presence of the Blessed One:
Life is swept along,
Short is the lifespan —
To old age we are led,
There is no stopping place.
Seeing this danger in death,
Do meritorious deeds
That bring true happiness.

Life is swept along,
Short is the lifespan —
To old age we are led,
There is no stopping place.
Seeing this danger in death,
Seeking peace, abandon worldly hopes.

title: Elder Puṇṇamāsa: Having abandoned the five hindrances, Attaining security from bondage, Holding the mirror of the Dhamma, Knowing and seeing the self. I contemplate this…
content:
Elder Puṇṇamāsa:

Having abandoned the five hindrances,
Attaining security from bondage,
Holding the mirror of the Dhamma,
Knowing and seeing the self.

I contemplate this body,
From within and without —
The body is seen as empty,
Both inside and out.

title: “Monks, while I was dwelling heedful, ardent, resolute, when a thought of renunciation arose, I understood: ‘This thought of renunciation has arisen in me, and…
content: “Monks, while I was dwelling heedful, ardent, resolute, when a thought of renunciation arose, I understood: ‘This thought of renunciation has arisen in me, and it leads neither to my own harm, nor to others’ harm, nor to the harm of both, increases wisdom, is not part of vexation, leads to Nibbāna.’ Monks, if I thought and pondered upon it at night, I saw no fear from that cause. If I thought and pondered upon it by day, I saw no fear from that cause. If I thought and pondered upon it both night and day, I saw no fear from that cause. But if I thought and pondered too long, my body might become fatigued; when the body is fatigued, the mind becomes disturbed; when the mind is disturbed, it is far from concentration. Then, monks, I steadied my mind internally, calmed it, unified it, concentrated it. Why was that? So that my mind would not be disturbed.”

title: “There are these two extremes that one who has gone forth should not pursue: devotion to sensual pleasure in sensual objects — low, vulgar, worldly,…
content:
“There are these two extremes that one who has gone forth should not pursue: devotion to sensual pleasure in sensual objects — low, vulgar, worldly, ignoble, unbeneficial; and devotion to self-mortification — painful, ignoble, unbeneficial. Avoiding these two extremes, the Middle Way has been realized by the Tathāgata, giving rise to vision, giving rise to knowledge, leading to peace, direct knowledge, enlightenment, Nibbāna.

And what, headman, is that Middle Way realized by the Tathāgata, giving rise to vision, giving rise to knowledge, leading to peace, direct knowledge, enlightenment, Nibbāna? It is the Noble Eightfold Path, namely: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration. This, headman, is the Middle Way realized by the Tathāgata, giving rise to vision, giving rise to knowledge, leading to peace, direct knowledge, enlightenment, Nibbāna.”

title: “Good is restraint over the eye, Good is restraint over the ear, Good is restraint over the nose, Good is restraint over the tongue.” “Good…
content:
“Good is restraint over the eye,
Good is restraint over the ear,
Good is restraint over the nose,
Good is restraint over the tongue.”

“Good is restraint over the body,
Good is restraint over speech,
Good is restraint over the mind,
Good is restraint everywhere.
A monk restrained everywhere
Is freed from all suffering.”

“One who controls his hands and feet,
Controls his speech and his head,
Delights in inner seclusion,
Is content, lives alone —
Him they call a monk.”

title: “Seeing the destruction of birth, The end of fetters, Destroying the path of sensual desire, Without remainder — That one is pure, faultless, Stainless, undefiled…
content:
“Seeing the destruction of birth,
The end of fetters,
Destroying the path of sensual desire,
Without remainder —
That one is pure, faultless,
Stainless, undefiled —
The Tathāgata is worthy of offerings.”

“One who does not see a self within the self,
Concentrated, upright, steady,
Without desire, without rigidity, without doubt —
The Tathāgata is worthy of offerings.”

“One in whom there is no root of delusion,
Who knows, who sees all things,
Who bears this last body —
Attaining perfect enlightenment,
The unsurpassed state of peace —
Thus is the Tathāgata, worthy of offerings.”

title: “Monks, what is Right Mindfulness? Monks, here a monk abides contemplating the body as a body, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having restrained covetousness and sorrow…
content: “Monks, what is Right Mindfulness? Monks, here a monk abides contemplating the body as a body, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having restrained covetousness and sorrow in the world; abides contemplating feelings as feelings … mind as mind … phenomena as phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having restrained covetousness and sorrow in the world. This, monks, is called Right Mindfulness.”

title: Hemavata: “Is he without desire for sensual pleasures? Is his mind undisturbed? Has he overcome all delusion? Does he truly have eyes for all things?”…
content:
Hemavata:
“Is he without desire for sensual pleasures?
Is his mind undisturbed?
Has he overcome all delusion?
Does he truly have eyes for all things?”

Sātāgira:
“He has no desire for sensual pleasures,
His mind is undisturbed,
He has overcome all delusion —
The Buddha truly has eyes for all things.”
